meaning: The single number that measures how wrong the network is on a batch. Training only ever follows its slope, so its shape decides how loudly each kind of mistake is corrected.
The average of squared errors (ŷ − y)². Its push grows with the error and its best constant guess is the mean; outliers dominate it, and behind a sigmoid it trains slowly when confidently wrong.
Squared error for small errors and absolute error beyond a threshold δ, so no single example can push harder than δ. Robust to outliers; used for bounding boxes.
−ln(probability the model gave to the right answer): the surprise at the truth. Behind sigmoid or softmax its gradient on the logits is simply p − y. A uniform guess over K classes scores ln K.
The raw score a network outputs before sigmoid or softmax turns it into a probability. PyTorch's classification losses expect logits, not probabilities.
Training against a softened target, (1 − ε) on the right class plus ε spread over all classes (ε = 0.1 is common), so the loss has a finite best confidence and logits stop growing.
The network written as a chain of tiny operations (multiply, add, ReLU…). The forward pass computes and caches values node by node; the backward pass walks it in reverse.
Computing every weight's gradient in one backward sweep: at each node, multiply its local derivative by the gradient arriving from above, adding up where paths merge.

Automatic differentiation that starts from the single loss and works backwards, so all gradients cost a small constant (typically 2–3×) times one forward pass, however many weights there are. The price is storing activations.
PyTorch's engine that records operations on tensors with requires_grad=True as your code runs, then computes gradients into each leaf's .grad, which accumulates until cleared.
Comparing a hand-written gradient with a centered finite difference (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h, with h ≈ 1e-5 in float64. A relative error around 1e-7 or less means the formula is right.
An n-dimensional array with a shape, a dtype and a device (CPU or GPU) that can record how it was computed. Batch dimension first by convention.
PyTorch's building block: an object with a forward() method whose assigned layers and nn.Parameters are registered automatically, so parameters(), to() and state_dict() find every weight.
Turns a dataset into shuffled mini-batches each epoch (optionally loading in parallel). Shuffling keeps each batch a fair sample of the data.
For each batch: forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step. Wrapped in model.train() for training and model.eval() plus torch.no_grad() for evaluation.
PyTorch's rule for combining tensors of different shapes by stretching size-1 dimensions. Useful, but (B, 1) minus (B,) silently becomes (B, B), a classic loss bug.
Why weights start random: units with identical starting weights get identical gradients and stay identical forever, so a layer of them acts like a single unit.
Random weights with variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out), which keeps signals and gradients at a steady size through tanh- or sigmoid-like layers.
Random weights with variance 2/fan_in. The factor 2 pays back the half of the signal that ReLU zeroes, so deep ReLU networks start with their signal intact.
Stepping along a running sum of past gradients instead of the latest one: consistent directions speed up (about 10× with β = 0.9) and zig-zags cancel.

An optimizer combining momentum with a per-weight step size (divide by the root of each weight's average squared gradient) plus bias correction. Works over a wide range of learning rates; stores two extra numbers per weight.
Adam with weight decay applied directly to the weights (w ← w − lr·λ·w) instead of as an L2 term in the gradient, which Adam would rescale. The default optimizer for transformers.
A 2024 optimizer for hidden-layer weight matrices that orthogonalizes the momentum update; used with AdamW for the other parameters (Kimi K2, nanochat).
How far each step moves the weights. The most important hyperparameter: too small crawls, too big diverges suddenly, and the best value sits just below that edge.
One short run with the learning rate growing every step, plotting loss against lr to see where it starts falling and where it blows up; a quick map for choosing the peak.
Ramping the learning rate up from near zero over the first steps (often 1–5% of training) so the network and Adam's statistics settle before full-size steps.
Lowering the learning rate from its peak along half a cosine wave, often to about 10% of the peak, so noisy mini-batch training settles into the minimum at the end.
A schedule that warms up, holds the peak constant for most of training, then decays over a short final stretch (about 10% of steps), so the run can be extended or stopped at any point.
A mini-batch is the B examples averaged for one gradient; a step is one optimizer update; an epoch is one pass over the data, N ÷ B steps. Gradient noise shrinks like 1/√B.
For SGD: when the batch size is multiplied by k, multiply the learning rate by k (with a gradual warmup). It lets large-batch training match small-batch accuracy, up to a limit.

term: Critical batch size / gradient noise scale
meaning: The batch size beyond which extra examples per step barely help, estimated by tr(Σ)/|G|²: per-example gradient variance over the squared true gradient. It grows as the loss falls.
Running k micro-batches with backward() (each loss divided by k) before one optimizer step, to get the gradient of a k× larger batch without the memory.
